div.head: Introductions
div.p: An industrial system for monitoring and controlling industrial plants is a distributed system which consists of many kinds of nodes such as operator stations, controllers, ITVs, and databases. The nodes in the system send various messages to other nodes, such as commands, video data, sounds, and data on plant conditions. One feature of ATM networks is the integration of various traffic into a single network. We will be able to construct industrial systems with simple network architecture using ATM technology. We believe that this simplicity will not only decrease the cost of each system but also make it easy to maintain the system.

Current ATM standards specified by the ATM Forum and ITU-T give us quality-of-service parameters such as transmission rates, cell loss rates, average (or statistical) delay times, and average delay jitters. They, however, rarely discuss either end-to-end delays or worst-case jitters or how to guarantee such parameters. On the other hand, we need to guarantee worstcase delivery times of messages in distributed industrial systems where operator stations issue commands to controllers for example.

Some theoretical studies of hard real-time communications in multi-hop networks like ATM networks have been carried out. Kandlur et al. [Kandlur 941 proposed the concept of a real-time channel which provides guarantees on the maximum delivery time for messages. They assumed that each switch node in a network performs traffic shaping for each channel.

The reason they need traffic shaping for each channel in output links of switch nodes is that they assume large scale general networks including many nodes. Channel jitters must be shaped by traffic shaping in output links of nodes. Otherwise, we cannot guarantee a minimum interarrival time of channels at input links of nodes.

On the other hand, industrial systems have networks whose scales are not so large. Figure 1 represents an example of an industrial system, which could be for a chemical plant for example, with an ATM network. The system consists of 6 sections. Each section has a large physical scale, usually a few hundred meters or even a few kilometers. One of the sections is a monitoring and controlling section where the operators work. Other sections are production sections where usually there is no one except when problems occur. Each section has an ATM switch in this example. If needed, a section can have more switches than one. The switches are connected to each other by links and form a 'ring' topology. This network topology depends on the physical topology of the plant where the products flow from one production section to another.

In the monitoring and controlling section, engineering work stations (EWSes), and operator stations (OPSen) are connected to the switch by links. The EWSes display video data sent from the production sections. The EWSes also receive piant data from the production sections and store the data onto disks. The stored data can be used by databases in the EWSes. The OlPSes receive plant data and display the data as trend graphs and so on. The OPSes can issue commands to the programable controllers (PCs) in the production sections. These commands can be driven not only by the operators but also automatically by the OI'Ses. In a production section, an industrial TV camera controller (ITVC) and programmable controllers (PCs are connected with the switch by links. to be monitored. The ITVC compresses video data sent from ITVs in a certain compression format (such as MPEG-I) and sends the compressed data to the monitoring and controlling section through the ATM network. The PCs are connected to actuators and sensors.

The minimum interarrival time of channels in in-Each ITVC h as several ITVs focused on the devices dustrial applications are usually of the order of several hundred milli-seconds while end-to-end delays are of a smaller order. We need no traffic shaping in switch nodes, if the end-to-end delay of a channel is smaller than its minimum interarrival time. To realize hard real-time communications in such a system, it is enough to statically prioritize the traffic. Even if a system is connected to a WAN via gateways, we can guarantee real-time communication in the system by assigning background priority to traffic to or from the WAN.

In this paper, we propose a method for a schedulability check in ATM networks which provides fixed prioritized virtual connections. Our method does not need any run-time scheduling other than fixed priority scheduling at each output link of all switch nodes and traffic shaping at each output link of all terminal nodes in a network. Rate monotonic analysis [Liu 731 and its extensions [Lehoczky 891 are known as schedulability check methods for tasks scheduled by a fixed priority policy. As described in Kandlur 94, we can use these methods for schedulability checks of real-time channels in multi-hop networks. These methods, however, as- sume a critical instance in which all tasks arrive at the same time. It is reasonable to consider the worst case in schedulability checks for tasks on CPUs, while it is not in those for messages in a network. We however can obtain information on the times when messages arrive at switch nodes in a network. Using such in- formation, our method can check schedulability for a set of channels more exactly than methods assuming a critical instance.

This paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we propose a method for schedulability checks in ATM networks which provide fixed prioritized virtual connections. We show an example in Section 3, and describe our future work in Section 4. Section 5 summarizes our work.
2 Proposed method

div.head: Preconditions
div.p: In this paper, we discuss unidirectional point-topoint communications which are connection oriented and have timing constraints. Such communications are called real-time channels [Kandlur 941. We do not discuss multi-cast communications here, but they can be realized with multiple real-time channels. We also can call a real-time channel a virtual connection (VC). Each real-time channel has the following parameters. 0 C: maximum size of messages. Suppose that transmission rate is constant and the sizes of messages are represented by their transmission times.
0 Psend: Minimum interarrival time for messages at the sender node.

0 Dreq: Worst case end-to-end delay required. At output links of switch nodes, ATM cells in VCs are scheduled by the priorities of the VCs. We do not discuss the routing of a new VC. This can be done by the signalling protocol which the ATM Forum has specified. The end-to-end delay of a VC is distributed to links in the route. At each link, the VC priorities are assigned according to deadline monotonic priority assignment, where a VC with a smaller delay at the link is assigned a higher priority. We assume that propagation delays and switching delays are small enough to be negligible compared with transmission delays and queuing delays at switch nodes.

Each sender terminal node must guarantee the parameters c and Psend of the Vcs. If an application program generates a message of a larger size than its parameter C, the message must be divided into several smaller ones or the sending of the message must be denied. If an application program generates messages in a shorter period than the parameter P s e n d , the sending of the messages must be delayed to guarantee the P.end (traffic shaping). Such a process against the violation of VC parameters can be done at any terminal node layer, such as network interface cards (NICs), OS, and the middleware between OS and the applications.

div.head: Basic algorithm
div.p: In this subsection, we propose a schedulability check method assuming a critical instance at each output link first. In Kandlur 94, a schedulability check method assuming a critical instance is described, but the method also assumes traffic shaping for each channel at the output links. Our method assumes no traffic shaping in switch nodes. Because of the lack of traffic shaping in switch nodes on its route, a channel enlarges its worst-case jitter link by link. div.head: Example
div.p: Here is an example of our method (as in figure 1). Table 1 represents all the real-time channels in the system. Each real-time channel has parameters, a route, a worst case end-to-end delay requirement, a minimum interarrival time for messages, and a maximum size of messages. Now let the link speed be 155 Mbps.

Using the proposed schedulability check method, we can theoretically guarantee that all real-time channels in table 1 will meet their deadline, i.e. the worst case end-to-end delay boundary. We also found by simulation that the case is actually schedulable. The simulator which we used is SES/Workbench.

div.head: Future work
div.p: The method proposed in this paper assumes that we cannot modify the delay constraints at links for a channel which has already been established (see table 2). There will be, however, some cases where the proposed method denies the schedulability for a set of channels while we can guarantee the schedulability by modifying the delay constraints at links for established channels. Modifying the delay constraints for established channels will make the problem of schedulability checks more difficult and complex. Not only solving this problem but also evaluating the exactness of the proposed method will be our future work.

To achieve real-time performance and reliability for distributed industrial systems, we must consider the management of many kinds of resource in the systems. For this purpose, we are now developing Resource Management for Distributed Control Systems (RM-DCS). The method proposed in this paper will be a part of RM-DCS: this means that the method will be used to manage several kinds of resource, such as buffer space, network bandwidth, and CPU for protocol processing, in systems. Distributed systems, however, include many other resources, such as CPUs for multimedia processing, system buses, or other devices, which musy be managed. In addition, industrial systems change their configuration for higher reliability and higher availability. We have already proposed a scheduling method for duplex-systems which perform reconfiguration [Mizunuma 941. We believe that we will be able to combine the two methods and extend them to manage all the resources to be managed in distributed industrial systems.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: In this paper, we propose a solution for real-time communication in industrial systems with ATM networks. We believe that we will be able to get all the plakforms, as commercial products, needed for our method in the very near future.
